title: How Heat Moves
bigQuestion: Why does the same food come out of the same oven browned and crisp one time and pale and soggy the next?

story.title: Two Trays, One Oven
story.kicker: Marcus and Jaylen roasted the same vegetables at the same temperature for the same time. Only one tray came out right.
paragraphs: The cooking lab had one assignment on the board: roasted vegetables, 425 °F, 25 minutes. Marcus and Jaylen worked at the same station. They cut the same bag of carrots, broccoli and red onion into pieces about an inch across, tossed them with 2 Tbsp of oil and a half teaspoon of salt, and split the bowl between two sheet pans. Both pans went into the same preheated oven on the same rack, side by side.

The difference was in how they loaded the pans. Marcus spread his vegetables in one layer with a little space between the pieces. Jaylen had cut a few extra carrots because he liked them, and he piled everything on, two and three pieces deep in the middle. "Same oven, same time," he said. "It will all cook."

At 12 minutes Ms. Okafor had them pull the oven door open and look. Marcus's pan was already sizzling. The edges of the onion had gone dark and sweet-smelling, and the cut faces of the carrots were turning brown. Jaylen's pan was wet. There was a shine of liquid on the bottom, and a puff of steam rolled out when the door opened. The vegetables were softening, but they were the same color they had been going in.

At 25 minutes the two pans came out. Marcus's broccoli had crisp brown tips and the carrots were tender with dark edges. Jaylen's vegetables were cooked through, but they were pale, limp and a little watery, and the ones in the middle of the pile were still firm. Same recipe, same oven, same timer.

"You did not roast those," Ms. Okafor told Jaylen, not unkindly. "You steamed them. Every vegetable is mostly water. Pile them up and the water they give off cannot escape, so the pan never gets hot enough on the surface of the food to brown it." She handed him a second sheet pan. "Next time, two pans. Crowding is the mistake almost every new cook makes, and it is the easiest one to fix."
story.think: Both pans sat in a 425 °F oven for 25 minutes. Where did the heat go on Jaylen's pan, and why did it not brown the vegetables?

lessons.title: Conduction: Pan to Food
lessons.mainIdea: Conduction is heat moving by direct touch, and it is why the side of the food that touches the pan is the side that browns.
reading: Set a dry skillet on a burner over medium heat and wait two minutes. The metal of the pan warms first where the flame or coil touches it, and the heat spreads outward through the metal. Lay a slice of bread in the pan. Within a minute the underside toasts while the top stays soft. Heat passed from the burner into the pan and from the pan into the bread by *conduction*: heat moving from one thing to another that it is touching.

Conduction only works where surfaces meet. That is why a steak browns only on the side pressed against the pan and why a pancake needs to be flipped. It is also why the shape of the food matters. A whole potato takes an hour to bake, but the same potato cut into half-inch cubes cooks in fifteen minutes. Heat has to travel from the outside of each piece to its center by conduction, and a thick piece has a long way to go.

Pans conduct heat at different speeds. Copper and aluminum move heat fast and evenly. Cast iron is slower to heat but holds heat well, so it does not cool off when cold food hits it. Stainless steel is sturdy but heats unevenly on its own, so good stainless pans have an aluminum or copper layer inside the base. A thin, cheap pan has hot spots right over the flame and cool spots at the edges, which is why food burns in the middle and stays pale at the rim.

Conduction also explains a common mistake. If you lay meat in a pan that is still cold, the meat warms slowly along with the pan, its juices leak out, and it ends up gray and steamed instead of brown. Heat the pan first, add the oil, and wait until the oil shimmers. Then add the food. The hot metal delivers heat to the surface fast enough to brown it before the inside overcooks.

words.d: heat moving directly from one thing into another that it touches, such as from a pan into a steak
a place on a thin pan directly over the burner that gets much hotter than the rest of the pan
the rippling look of oil in a pan when it is hot enough to add food

look.title: One Potato, Three Ways
look.text: Three cooks each have one russet potato and a 400 °F oven. Cook A puts the potato in whole. Cook B cuts it in half lengthwise and lays it cut side down on a sheet pan. Cook C cuts it into half-inch cubes and spreads them out. All three check at 20 minutes. Only Cook C's potato is done, and it has brown edges. Cook B's is soft a half inch in and hard in the center. Cook A's is still raw inside.
look.prompt: Explain each result using conduction. What would you tell Cook A to do if dinner is in 30 minutes?

check.q: A cook lays chicken thighs in a cold pan, then turns on the burner. What is the most likely result?
choices: The skin browns evenly
The chicken cooks faster than normal
The chicken leaks juice and turns gray instead of brown
The pan warps
check.why: A cold pan cannot deliver heat fast enough to brown the surface. The meat warms slowly, loses juice and steams in it.

check.q: Why do half-inch potato cubes cook far faster than a whole potato at the same temperature?
choices: Cutting releases starch that cooks faster
Heat only has to travel a short distance by conduction to reach the center of each cube
Small pieces absorb more oil
The oven is hotter near small pieces
check.why: Conduction moves heat from the surface inward. A short path means the center is done sooner.

check.q: Which pan is most likely to burn food in the middle while leaving the edges pale?
choices: A thin, lightweight pan
A heavy cast-iron skillet
A stainless pan with an aluminum core
A copper pan
check.why: Thin pans have hot spots directly over the burner. Heavy or layered pans spread heat more evenly.

lessons.title: Convection: Moving Air and Water
lessons.mainIdea: Convection carries heat through moving air, water or oil, which is why a convection oven cooks faster and why boiling water cooks evenly on every side.
reading: Drop a handful of pasta into a pot of boiling water. Every piece is surrounded by water at 212 °F, top, bottom and sides, and every piece cooks at the same rate. That is *convection*: heat carried by a moving liquid or gas. In the pot, hot water rises from the bottom, cooler water sinks to take its place, and the whole pot keeps circulating. Nothing has to touch the pan directly to get hot.

An oven works by convection too, just with air instead of water. The heating element warms the air, the warm air rises and moves, and the food is surrounded by hot air on all sides. Air carries heat much less efficiently than water does, which is why you can reach into a 350 °F oven for a moment but never into 212 °F water. A *convection oven* adds a fan that blows the hot air around. Moving air strips away the layer of cooler, damp air that clings to food, so it browns faster and more evenly. Many recipes say to lower the temperature about 25 °F when using the fan.

Deep frying is convection in oil. Oil can be heated far past 212 °F, usually to 350 or 375 °F, and it flows around the food just like water. The surface of the food dries and browns quickly while the moisture inside turns to steam and cooks it from within. That is why fried food is crisp outside and soft inside.

Convection needs room to move. In a boiling pot, too much pasta in too little water drops the temperature and the pieces stick together. In an oven, a pan pushed against the wall or two racks stacked close together block the air and leave cool pockets. Leave space around pans and rotate them halfway through baking so every side sees moving air.

words.d: heat carried by a moving liquid or gas, such as boiling water or the hot air in an oven
an oven with a fan that moves the hot air, so food browns faster and more evenly
to move around in a loop, as hot water rises and cooler water sinks in a pot

look.title: Heat by Convection: Common Working Temperatures
rows: water at a rolling boil (sea level)
convection oven, same recipe, fan on
look.cite: Standard kitchen figures; the 25 °F convection reduction is a common recipe rule
look.prompt: Oil at 350 °F is hotter than boiling water, yet fried food does not get as hot inside as 350 °F. Where does the heat go?

check.q: Why does a convection oven brown food faster than a regular oven set to the same temperature?
choices: It uses a hotter heating element
The fan moves the air, sweeping away the cooler, damp layer that clings to the food
It has a smaller inside
It heats by conduction instead of convection
check.why: Moving air transfers heat faster than still air. The fan keeps fresh hot air against the food's surface.

check.q: Two sheet pans of cookies are baked on two racks close together. The bottom pan's cookies are pale on top. Why?
choices: The upper pan blocks the flow of hot air to the lower pan
The bottom rack is always cooler
The cookies were too small
The oven was not preheated
check.why: Oven heat is convection. A pan directly above another blocks the air that would brown the lower tray.

check.q: A recipe written for a regular oven says 375 °F. You have a convection oven. What is the usual adjustment?
choices: Raise it to 400 °F
Double the time
Lower it to about 350 °F
Bake with the door cracked open
check.why: The common rule is to reduce the temperature by about 25 °F when the fan is on, because moving air cooks faster.

lessons.title: Radiation: Heat Across Space
lessons.mainIdea: Radiant heat travels in straight lines from a glowing element or coals to whatever faces it, which is why the broiler cooks only the top and the grill cooks only the bottom.
reading: Hold your hand a few inches below the glowing coil of a broiler, not touching anything, and you feel the heat right away. Nothing hot is touching your hand and the air is barely moving. The heat is arriving as *radiation*: energy that travels in straight lines from a hot surface to whatever faces it, the same way sunlight warms your face. A toaster, a broiler, a grill and a campfire all cook mostly by radiant heat.

Radiant heat only reaches the side of the food that faces the source, and it weakens quickly with distance. Under a broiler, the top of a piece of fish browns and the bottom does not. On a grill, the underside chars while the top stays pale until you flip it. Moving food two inches closer to a broiler makes a large difference; moving it four inches away can turn broiling into gentle warming. That is why broiler recipes tell you which rack position to use.

In a regular oven, radiation and convection work together. The walls and the bottom element radiate heat while the air carries it. A dark metal pan absorbs more radiant heat than a shiny one, so cookies on a dark pan brown faster on the bottom and can burn. A glass baking dish lets radiant heat pass through to the food, so many recipes say to lower the oven by 25 °F when baking in glass.

Microwaves are a special kind of radiation. The oven sends out waves that make water molecules in the food vibrate, and that vibration is heat. Microwaves heat the water inside the food directly, an inch or so deep, rather than heating the surface first. That is why microwaved food does not brown and why it can be scalding in one spot and cold in another. Stir, cover and let food stand a minute so the heat evens out.

words.d: heat that travels in straight lines from a hot source to whatever faces it, like a broiler or the sun
the heating element at the top of an oven that cooks food from above with intense radiant heat
an oven that heats the water inside food directly with waves, without browning the surface

look.title: Fish Under the Broiler
look.text: A cook slides a pan of salmon fillets under the broiler on the top rack, about three inches from the element, and sets a timer for 8 minutes without looking. At 6 minutes, smoke drifts out. The top of each fillet is black at the thick end and the thin tail ends are burnt through, while the bottom of the thick pieces is still translucent. The cook says the broiler must be broken.
look.prompt: Using what you know about radiant heat and distance, explain what actually happened and give two changes for next time.

check.q: Why does broiled food brown only on top?
choices: The pan blocks the air
Radiant heat travels in straight lines and reaches only the side facing the element
The bottom of the food is wetter
Broilers are cooler than ovens
check.why: A broiler is radiant heat from above. Only the surface that faces the element receives it.

check.q: Cookies on a dark metal sheet come out burnt on the bottom while the same dough on a shiny sheet is fine. What explains it?
choices: Dark metal is thinner
Dark metal reflects heat into the dough
The oven has a hot spot
Dark metal absorbs more radiant heat than shiny metal
check.why: Dark surfaces absorb radiant heat; shiny surfaces reflect it. The dark pan's bottom gets hotter.

check.q: Leftover chili from the microwave is boiling at the edge and cold in the center. What is the best fix?
choices: Stir it, cover it, and heat again until it reaches 165 °F throughout
Use a metal bowl
Heat it uncovered on high for twice as long
Eat the hot edges first
check.why: Microwaves heat unevenly. Stirring spreads the heat, and leftovers must reach 165 °F all the way through.

lessons.title: Preheating Pays Off
lessons.mainIdea: Preheating the oven, the pan and the grill puts full heat on the surface of the food from the first second, which is what browning and good texture depend on.
reading: Turn the oven to 425 °F and the display reads 425 °F within seconds. The oven is not there yet. The display shows the setting, not the temperature. Most home ovens take 15 to 20 minutes to come up to a roasting temperature, and the walls and racks take longer still. Many ovens beep when the air near the sensor reaches the setting, which is before the walls have caught up. Give it a few extra minutes after the beep, and use an oven thermometer hung from the middle rack if you want the truth.

Why does it matter? Roasted vegetables, bread, cookies and pizza all depend on a burst of high heat in the first minutes. Vegetables put into a cold oven sit in their own moisture as it slowly warms and end up soft and pale. A loaf of bread needs high heat right away to spring up before its crust sets. Cookies spread and go flat in an oven that is still warming. Preheating also makes timing honest: a recipe's 25 minutes assumes the oven was already at temperature.

Pans need preheating too. For sautéing, heat the empty pan over medium-high for a minute or two, add the oil, and wait until it shimmers and flows like water. A drop of water flicked in should sizzle and dance. Cast iron takes longer, five minutes or more, because it heats slowly. A grill needs 10 to 15 minutes with the lid closed so the grates are hot enough to sear grill marks and release the food instead of gluing it.

There are exceptions. Braises, casseroles and a whole roast that will cook for hours do not need a screaming-hot start, and a few recipes call for a cold-oven start on purpose. Pastry and dough that must stay cold, such as pie crust, go into a fully preheated oven so the butter turns to steam before it melts out. Read the recipe, and when it says preheat, do it first, before you start chopping.

words.d: to bring an oven, pan or grill fully up to temperature before the food goes in
a small thermometer that hangs or stands inside the oven and shows its real temperature
to brown the surface of food quickly on very high heat

look.title: The Recipe Says 25 Minutes
look.text: Dani turns the oven to 425 °F, cuts vegetables for ten minutes, and puts the pan in as soon as the oven beeps. She sets a timer for 25 minutes. When it rings, the vegetables are soft but not brown. The next day she turns the oven on first, cuts the vegetables, waits five minutes after the beep, and puts the pan in. Same timer. This time the edges are dark and crisp.
look.prompt: What changed between the two days, and why did the recipe's time only work on the second day?

check.q: The oven beeps to say it has reached 400 °F. What is the safest assumption?
choices: The oven walls and racks are at 400 °F
The air near the sensor is close, but the walls need a few more minutes
The oven is above 400 °F and should be turned down
The food can be placed in a cold oven instead
check.why: The beep means the air at the sensor hit the setting. The walls and racks lag behind, so wait a few minutes.

check.q: Which food most needs a fully preheated oven?
choices: A pot roast braising for three hours
A casserole warming through
A loaf of bread that needs to rise quickly before its crust sets
A pan of beans simmering with a lid
check.why: Bread's rise in the oven depends on immediate high heat. Slow, long-cooked dishes forgive a cool start.

check.q: How do you know a skillet with oil is hot enough for sautéing?
choices: The oil is smoking heavily
The pan has been on the burner for exactly 30 seconds
The oil looks the same as when it was poured in
The oil shimmers and a drop of water sizzles at once
check.why: Shimmering oil that sizzles a drop of water is ready. Heavy smoke means the oil is too hot and breaking down.

lessons.title: Roasting and Baking
lessons.mainIdea: Roasting and baking surround food with hot, dry air in an oven, and high heat with space around the food is what makes the surface brown and crisp.
reading: Roasting and baking are the same method with two names. Both cook food uncovered in the dry, hot air of an oven. Cooks usually say *roast* for meat and vegetables and *bake* for bread, pastry and casseroles, but the oven does not know the difference. Because the air is dry, the surface of the food dries out and then browns. That browning is what gives roasted chicken its skin and a roasted carrot its sweet, dark edges.

Here is a basic vegetable roast. Preheat the oven to 425 °F. Cut vegetables into even pieces about an inch across so they finish together. Toss them in a bowl with about 1 Tbsp of oil per pound and a half teaspoon of salt. Spread them in a single layer on a rimmed sheet pan with space between the pieces, cut sides down where you can, since the cut face against the hot metal browns best. Roast 20 to 30 minutes, turning once halfway, until the edges are dark and a fork slides in easily.

Meat roasts by the same rules but on a rack or a bed of vegetables so air reaches every side. A high temperature, 400 to 450 °F, browns the outside; a moderate one, 325 to 375 °F, cooks the inside gently. Many cooks use both, starting hot and turning the oven down, or finishing hot. Whatever the plan, the thermometer decides when it is done: 165 °F for poultry, 145 °F with a 3-minute rest for whole cuts of beef, pork and lamb.

The mistakes are the usual ones. Crowding traps steam and stops browning. Skipping the oil leaves the surface dry and leathery instead of crisp, because oil conducts heat into the surface and carries flavor. Cutting pieces in different sizes means the small ones burn before the large ones are done. Opening the oven door every few minutes drops the temperature and throws off the timing.

words.d: to cook uncovered in the dry heat of an oven, usually at a high temperature, so the surface browns
the same oven method as roasting; the word cooks use for bread, pastry and casseroles
a flat metal pan with a low edge, used for roasting vegetables in one layer
food cut to the same size so every piece finishes cooking at the same time

look.title: Order the Roast
look.text: Here are the steps of a vegetable roast out of order: turn the pieces halfway through; toss with oil and salt; preheat the oven to 425 °F; check with a fork for tenderness; cut into inch-sized pieces; spread in one layer with space between pieces; roast 20 to 30 minutes.
look.prompt: Put the steps in the right order and say which one, if skipped, turns roasting into steaming.

check.q: Why should roasted vegetables be tossed with oil before going in the oven?
choices: Oil carries heat into the surface and helps it brown and crisp
Oil keeps them from cooking too fast
Oil adds water to the pan
Oil is only for flavor and can always be skipped
check.why: A thin coat of oil conducts heat into the surface, which browns instead of drying out leathery.

check.q: A pork loin roast reads 145 °F on the thermometer. What comes next?
choices: Cook it to 165 °F to be safe
Let it rest 3 minutes before carving
Slice it immediately
Return it to the oven for 20 minutes
check.why: Whole cuts of pork are safe at 145 °F followed by a 3-minute rest. That is the USDA figure.

check.q: Roasted potatoes come out with the small pieces burnt and the large pieces raw in the center. What went wrong?
choices: The oven was too cool
Too much oil was used
There was too much salt
The pieces were cut to different sizes
check.why: Heat travels inward by conduction, so pieces of different sizes finish at different times. Cut evenly.

lessons.title: Sautéing and Pan-Frying
lessons.mainIdea: Sautéing cooks small pieces fast in a little fat in a hot pan, and it only works if the pan is hot, the food is dry, and there is room for steam to escape.
reading: Sauté comes from a French word for jump, and that is the picture: small pieces of food tossed in a hot pan with a little fat until they are browned and cooked through. Here is how to sauté sliced mushrooms. Heat a wide skillet over medium-high for about two minutes. Add 1 Tbsp of oil and let it shimmer. Add the mushrooms in a single layer and do not touch them for a full minute so the undersides brown. Then stir or toss, add a pinch of salt, and cook until they are golden, 5 to 7 minutes.

Three things make a sauté succeed. First, a hot pan, so the surface of the food browns before the inside overcooks. Second, dry food. Pat vegetables and meat dry with a paper towel; water on the surface must boil away before browning can start, and it cools the pan while it does. Third, space. If the pan is crowded, the food gives off steam faster than it can escape, the temperature drops, and the food boils in its own juices. Cook in batches if you must.

*Pan-frying* is the bigger cousin of sautéing. The pieces are larger, such as a chicken cutlet or a pork chop, the fat is deeper, about a quarter inch, and the heat is a step lower, medium to medium-high, so the outside does not burn before the center is done. Lay food into the pan away from you so hot fat does not splash toward your hand. Turn once, when the first side is deeply brown and the food releases from the pan on its own.

Fat choice matters. Butter tastes wonderful but burns above medium heat because of its milk solids; use it for gentle sautéing or add it at the end. Neutral oils such as canola or vegetable oil handle high heat. Olive oil works for most sautéing. If any fat starts to smoke heavily, pull the pan off the heat, let it cool a moment, and lower the burner. Never add water to hot fat, and keep a lid nearby in case of a flare-up.

words.d: to cook small pieces quickly in a little hot fat in a wide pan, tossing or stirring
to cook larger pieces in a shallow layer of fat at medium to medium-high heat, turning once
cooking part of the food at a time so the pan is never crowded
the moment browned food lets go of the pan on its own, showing the first side is done

look.title: Chicken That Stuck
look.text: Leo puts 1 Tbsp of oil in a cold pan, turns the burner to medium, and adds four chicken cutlets straight from the package, still wet, filling the pan edge to edge. After three minutes he tries to flip them. They tear and stick, the pan is full of cloudy liquid, and nothing is brown. He turns the heat to high to fix it, and the liquid boils off and the bottoms burn while the tops are still pink.
look.prompt: Name every mistake Leo made, in order, and write the steps he should follow next time.

check.q: Mushrooms in a sauté pan are sitting in liquid and not browning. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Too little salt
The pan was crowded, so steam could not escape and the pan cooled
The mushrooms were sliced too thin
Olive oil was used instead of butter
check.why: Crowding traps steam and drops the pan temperature. The food boils in its own juice instead of browning.

check.q: Why pat meat dry before it goes into a hot pan?
choices: Surface water must boil away before browning can begin, and it cools the pan
Wet meat absorbs too much oil
Water makes the meat tough
Dry meat needs less salt
check.why: Browning needs a surface hotter than 212 °F. Water on the surface holds it at the boiling point until it is gone.

check.q: Which fat is the poor choice for high-heat sautéing, and why?
choices: Canola oil, because it has no flavor
Vegetable oil, because it smokes at a low temperature
Butter, because its milk solids burn above medium heat
Olive oil, because it cannot be heated
check.why: Butter's milk solids scorch at high heat. Use it for gentle cooking or add it at the end for flavor.

lessons.title: Grilling and Broiling
lessons.mainIdea: Grilling and broiling cook with intense radiant heat from one side, which suits thin, tender foods and demands close attention and a flip.
reading: Grilling and broiling are the same idea turned upside down. On a grill, radiant heat from coals or burners comes from below. Under a broiler, it comes from the element above. Both are hot and fast, both brown only the side facing the heat, and both are best for foods that cook through quickly: burgers, chicken pieces, fish fillets, vegetables cut into slabs, thin steaks and chops. A thick roast or a tough cut needs a gentler method.

To broil, set a rack so the food will be about 4 inches from the element, and preheat the broiler for 5 minutes with the door closed. Put the food on a broiler pan or a rimmed sheet, pat it dry and oil it lightly. Slide it in and stay in the kitchen. Broiling is measured in minutes, and a piece of fish can go from pale to burnt in the time it takes to answer a text. Turn once, and check doneness with a thermometer: 165 °F for chicken, 160 °F for a burger, 145 °F for fish.

To grill, preheat with the lid closed for 10 to 15 minutes, then scrape the grates with a brush and wipe them with an oiled paper towel held in tongs. Lay food on the hot grates and leave it alone until it releases and shows dark marks, then turn. Set up two zones if you can, one hot and one cooler, so food that browns too fast can be moved to finish gently. Use long tongs, keep a spray bottle of water for small flare-ups on charcoal, and never squirt water at a grease fire on a gas grill; close the lid and turn off the burners.

Safety around grills is not optional. Grill outdoors only, never in a garage or under an overhang; the carbon monoxide from charcoal and gas is deadly indoors. Keep children and pets three feet away. Use one plate and one set of tongs for raw meat and a clean plate for cooked, so juices from raw chicken never touch the finished food. Let coals cool completely before disposing of them.

words.d: to cook on a grate over radiant heat from below, from coals or gas burners
to cook under the radiant heat of the element at the top of an oven
a grill set up with one hot side for searing and one cooler side for finishing gently
a sudden burst of flame when fat drips onto hot coals or burners

look.title: Grill and Broiler Doneness Temperatures
rows: steak or pork chop, then rest 3 min
look.prompt: A burger and a steak are the same thickness and the same color inside. Why does the burger need a higher temperature?

check.q: Grease flares up on a gas grill. What is the right first move?
choices: Spray it with water
Fan it with the lid to cool it
Move the food to the hot zone
Close the lid and turn off the burners
check.why: Water spreads a grease fire. Closing the lid starves it of air, and shutting off the gas removes the fuel.

check.q: Which food is best suited to broiling?
choices: A four-pound beef chuck roast
A thin fish fillet
A pot of dried beans
A whole pumpkin
check.why: Broiling is intense heat from one side for a short time. It suits thin, tender foods that cook through in minutes.

check.q: Why should a grill never be used in a garage with the door open?
choices: The heat will crack the concrete
Carbon monoxide from the fuel can build up and poison people indoors
The smoke will stain the walls
The grill will not get hot enough
check.why: Charcoal and gas grills give off carbon monoxide, which is deadly in an enclosed space, even with a door open.

lessons.title: Boiling, Simmering, Poaching, Steaming
lessons.mainIdea: Moist-heat methods cook food in or over water at or below 212 °F, and the difference between boiling, simmering and poaching is how much the water is moving.
reading: Water sets a ceiling. At sea level it boils at 212 °F and cannot get hotter as a liquid, no matter how high the burner is. That is why nothing browns in a pot of water, and it is why moist-heat cooking is gentle and forgiving. The choice among the moist methods comes down to how much the water is moving, which you can see. A *boil* has big, rolling bubbles breaking all over the surface. A *simmer* has small bubbles rising lazily, a few at a time. A *poach* has almost no bubbles at all, just a shimmer, with the water well below boiling.

Use a rolling boil for pasta and for blanching green vegetables, where you want speed and the water's movement keeps pieces from sticking. Use a simmer for soups, stews, dried beans, rice and anything that cooks a long time; a hard boil would break the food apart and boil away the liquid. Use a poach for delicate food that would fall apart or toughen: eggs, fish, chicken breast. Bring the liquid to a bare simmer, add the food, and hold the heat low.

*Steaming* cooks food over boiling water, not in it. Put an inch of water in a pot, set a steamer basket above the waterline, bring the water to a boil, add the food and cover. Steam surrounds the food at 212 °F and cooks it fast without washing away flavor or nutrients into the water. Broccoli steams in about 5 minutes, and green beans in about 5 to 7. Open the lid away from your face; a cloud of steam burns worse than boiling water because it carries more heat.

Common mistakes are easy to spot. Boiling a stew hard turns the meat stringy and the vegetables to mush. Salting pasta water lightly or not at all leaves it bland; use about 1 Tbsp of salt per 4 quarts. Letting a steamer boil dry scorches the pot and can crack it. And a pot that is too small for the pasta drops back to a simmer when the pasta goes in, so the pieces glue together at the bottom.

words.d: water at 212 °F with large bubbles rolling and breaking across the whole surface
liquid just below boiling, with small bubbles rising slowly a few at a time
to cook gently in liquid well below boiling, with barely a bubble
to cook food in a covered pot above boiling water, so the vapor cooks it
to boil vegetables briefly, then plunge them into ice water to stop the cooking

look.title: Read the Pot
look.text: Four pots sit on four burners. Pot 1: the surface heaves and big bubbles burst everywhere, and a rattling lid lets out steam. Pot 2: a few small bubbles drift up near the edge every second or two. Pot 3: the surface is still and glossy, with a wisp of steam and no bubbles. Pot 4: a basket sits above an inch of hard-boiling water, lid on, with steam escaping around the rim.
look.prompt: Name each method. Then assign a food to each pot: eggs out of the shell, dried pasta, beef stew, and broccoli florets.

check.q: A cook wants to poach eggs. What should the water look like when the eggs go in?
choices: Barely moving, with almost no bubbles
A rolling boil
Cold, then brought up to a boil
Boiling hard with a lid on
check.why: Poaching is gentle heat well below boiling. Rolling water tears delicate food apart.

check.q: A beef stew was cooked at a hard boil for two hours. What is the likely result?
choices: Tender meat and a rich sauce
Meat that is stringy and vegetables that fell apart
Meat that is still raw in the center
A sauce that is too thin because nothing evaporated
check.why: Stews need a simmer. A hard boil toughens meat fibers, breaks up vegetables and boils away the liquid.

check.q: What is the safe way to open a lid on a pot of steaming vegetables?
choices: Lean over it to see if it is done
Lift the lid straight up quickly
Tilt the lid so it opens away from your face
Remove it with a wet towel
check.why: Steam carries more heat than boiling water and burns badly. Open the lid away from you so the cloud escapes on the far side.

lessons.title: Braising and Stewing
lessons.mainIdea: Braising and stewing brown the food first in dry heat, then finish it slowly in a little liquid with a lid, which makes tough cuts tender.
reading: Some of the best-tasting dishes use two kinds of heat, one after the other. *Braising* starts by browning a large piece of meat or a batch of vegetables in a hot pan with a little fat. Then liquid is added, only partway up the food, the pot is covered, and it cooks slowly at a low simmer, on the stovetop or in a 300 to 325 °F oven, until it is fork-tender. *Stewing* is the same idea with food cut into bite-sized pieces and enough liquid to cover them. Both are called combination methods because dry heat does the browning and moist heat does the tenderizing.

Here is the shape of a braise. Pat the meat dry and season it with salt. Heat 1 to 2 Tbsp of oil in a heavy pot over medium-high until it shimmers. Brown the meat on all sides, taking your time, about 3 to 4 minutes per side, and do not crowd the pot. Set the meat aside. Cook chopped onion, carrot and celery in the same pot until soft. Add liquid, such as broth, and scrape up the brown bits stuck to the bottom. Return the meat, bring the liquid to a simmer, cover, and cook low and slow for two to three hours.

Time is the secret. Tough cuts such as chuck, shoulder and shank are full of connective tissue, the tough web that holds muscle together. Fast cooking leaves it chewy. Long, gentle, moist heat slowly turns it into gelatin, which is silky and rich, and the meat falls apart. Rush it with a hard boil and the muscle fibers seize up and dry out before the connective tissue has time to soften. Check every hour, keep the liquid at a lazy simmer, and add a splash more if it runs low.

Braises and stews reward planning. They taste better the next day, so they suit cooking ahead. Cool them within two hours of cooking, refrigerate at 40 °F or below, and reheat to 165 °F. Skim the fat that rises and hardens on top before reheating if you like a lighter sauce. Leftover braising liquid is the base for a great soup.

words.d: to brown food, then cook it slowly, covered, in a small amount of liquid until tender
to brown bite-sized pieces, then simmer them covered in enough liquid to cover
a method that uses dry heat to brown and moist heat to finish, such as braising
the tough web that holds muscle together; slow moist heat turns it into soft gelatin
cooked until a fork slides in and the meat pulls apart with no resistance

look.title: Braising a Beef Chuck Roast: An Example Time Plan
look.cite: Example plan for a 3-pound chuck roast; times vary with the cut
look.prompt: Add up the total. If dinner is at 6:30, what time must the browning start?

check.q: What is the difference between braising and stewing?
choices: Braising uses a large piece with liquid partway up; stewing uses small pieces covered in liquid
Braising has no browning step
Stewing is done uncovered
Stewing uses dry heat only
check.why: Both brown, then simmer covered. Braising is a whole piece partly submerged; stewing is bite-sized pieces fully covered.

check.q: Why does a tough cut become tender after three hours of gentle braising?
choices: The liquid soaks into the meat
The fat melts and replaces the muscle
Slow moist heat turns connective tissue into gelatin
The salt breaks down the muscle fibers
check.why: Connective tissue turns to gelatin only with time and gentle moist heat. That is what makes the meat fall apart.

check.q: A cook is braising a chuck roast and is running late, so she turns the burner to high and boils it. What happens?
choices: The roast is done sooner and just as tender
The muscle fibers seize and dry out before the connective tissue softens
The liquid turns to gelatin
The pot becomes safer to leave alone
check.why: A hard boil toughens meat. Braising cannot be rushed; it needs a lazy simmer and time.

lessons.title: The Crowded Pan
lessons.mainIdea: Food is mostly water, and if the water it gives off cannot escape, the pan never gets hotter than 212 °F on the food's surface and nothing browns.
reading: Go back to Jaylen's pan. A raw carrot is close to 90 percent water, and mushrooms, zucchini and onions are about the same. As they heat, that water turns to steam and leaves the surface. On a pan with space, the steam floats away, the surface dries, and the temperature of the food's skin climbs past 212 °F toward the oven's 425 °F. Then it browns. On a crowded pan, steam from one piece condenses on its neighbor. The food sits in a wet fog at 212 °F, which is exactly the temperature of a steamer basket.

The same thing happens on the stovetop, faster. A skillet holds only so much heat. Every cold, wet piece of food you drop in pulls heat out of the metal. Add too many at once and the pan's temperature crashes below the point where water boils off quickly. Juice pools, the food gray-steams, and by the time the liquid finally cooks away the inside is overdone. That is why recipes say in batches, why a good sauté pan is heavy, and why the first batch should always be smaller than you think.

The fix is space, and it is cheap. On a sheet pan, leave a finger's width between pieces and use two pans instead of one; put them on two racks and swap and rotate halfway through. In a skillet, cook the food in two or three rounds and set the finished ones on a plate; they reheat in seconds when everything goes back together at the end. For meat, one piece per hand-sized area of pan is a fair rule. For a big crowd, roast at a higher temperature rather than piling more on a pan.

Wet food is crowded food's twin. Vegetables straight from the colander carry a film of water that must boil off before browning starts. Spin salad greens dry, pat vegetables and meat with a towel, and let frozen vegetables thaw and drain before they hit the oil. A dry surface, a hot pan, and room to breathe: those three things are the difference between roasted and steamed.

words.d: putting so much food in a pan that steam cannot escape and the pan cools, so nothing browns
when steam cools and turns back into liquid water on a nearby surface
to turn a pan around and swap racks halfway through baking so every side gets even heat

look.title: Five Pounds of Potatoes, One Oven
look.text: A student has to roast five pounds of cubed potatoes for a class dinner. She has two sheet pans, two oven racks and 45 minutes. Her first plan is to heap all the potatoes on one pan and roast at 400 °F. Her friend suggests splitting them across both pans, raising the oven to 450 °F, and swapping the pans top-to-bottom and front-to-back at the halfway mark.
look.prompt: Predict the result of each plan and explain, using water and steam, why the second one browns.

check.q: On a crowded sheet pan, about what temperature is the surface of the vegetables during most of the cooking?
choices: 425 °F, the oven setting
About 212 °F, because they sit in their own steam
About 140 °F
Room temperature
check.why: Trapped steam keeps the food's surface at the boiling point of water. Browning needs the surface to climb well past 212 °F.

check.q: A recipe for sautéed chicken serves eight, but the pan fits four pieces with space. What should the cook do?
choices: Fit all eight and cook longer
Add water so the pieces cook evenly
Cook in two batches and set the first batch aside
Lower the heat and cover the pan
check.why: Batches keep the pan hot and the food dry. The first batch reheats in moments at the end.

check.q: Which pair of conditions is needed for browning?
choices: A dry surface and a hot pan with room around the food
A wet surface and a cold pan
A lid and a low burner
Cold food straight from the fridge in a crowded pan
check.why: Browning needs the surface dry and hotter than 212 °F. Water, crowding and a cool pan all prevent it.

lessons.title: Maillard and Caramelization
lessons.mainIdea: Browning is two chemical changes, the Maillard reaction between proteins and sugars and the caramelization of sugar alone, and both need dry heat well above the boiling point of water.
reading: Why does a seared steak taste different from a boiled one made of the same meat? The answer is the *Maillard reaction*, named for the French chemist who described it. When a food that contains both proteins and sugars, which is almost every food, gets hot and dry enough, those molecules react with each other and form hundreds of new compounds. Those compounds are the brown color and the deep, roasted, savory flavors of bread crust, seared meat, toasted nuts and roasted coffee. The reaction gets going quickly only above roughly 300 °F, which is why a wet surface at 212 °F stays pale.

*Caramelization* is a different change with a similar look. It happens when sugar itself is heated until it breaks apart and rebuilds into new molecules, giving the deep amber color and the nutty, slightly bitter taste of caramel. It needs even higher heat than Maillard, starting well above 300 °F. Onions cooked slowly until they are soft and sweet and brown are caramelized; the sugar in the onion has changed. The dark edge on a roasted sweet potato is both reactions at once.

Both reactions explain the rules you already know. Preheat, because the surface must reach browning temperature fast. Dry the food, because water holds the surface at 212 °F. Do not crowd, because steam does the same. Use a little fat, because it conducts heat into the surface and carries the flavor compounds. And do not move the food too soon; the browned crust forms in the first minute or two of stillness, and then it releases from the pan on its own.

Browning has a limit. Go past it and the same reactions run to black char, which tastes bitter and acrid. Toast is delicious; burnt toast is not. Watch the color, not just the timer, and pull food when it is deep golden brown. If a pan's brown bits, called fond, have gone black, they will make any sauce bitter, so wipe them out and start again rather than trying to save them.

words.d: the browning reaction between proteins and sugars on hot, dry food that creates roasted, savory flavor
the browning of sugar itself at high heat, giving amber color and nutty, slightly bitter flavor
the browned bits stuck to the bottom of a pan after searing; the base of a pan sauce
food burned black past the point of browning, which tastes bitter

look.title: An 1896 Cook on the Value of Browning
look.text: Fannie Farmer's 1896 cookbook advised searing meat quickly on all sides in a hot pan first, explaining that the browned surface holds in the juices, and only then cooking it more slowly. Cooks later learned that a seared crust does not actually seal in juice, but that the browned surface is where most of the roasted flavor comes from.
look.cite: Fannie Merritt Farmer, The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book, 1896 (paraphrased and summarized)
look.prompt: Farmer was right that searing improves meat but wrong about why. What is the real reason, in one sentence?

check.q: What two kinds of molecules react in the Maillard reaction?
choices: Fats and water
Proteins and sugars
Salt and acid
Starch and fat
check.why: Maillard browning is a reaction between proteins (amino acids) and sugars on a hot, dry surface.

check.q: Onions cooked slowly until deep brown and sweet are an example of what?
choices: Steaming
Poaching
Blanching
Caramelization
check.why: The onion's own sugars break down and rebuild at high heat into the sweet, amber compounds of caramel.

check.q: Why can food never brown while it sits in liquid?
choices: Liquid washes away the proteins
Sugar dissolves in water
The surface cannot get hotter than 212 °F while water is present, and browning needs far more
The pan is too heavy
check.why: Water caps the surface at its boiling point. Maillard and caramelization need dry heat well above that.

review.q: Which method moves heat by direct contact between the pan and the food?
choices: Convection
Radiation
Conduction
Microwaving
review.why: Conduction is heat passing between things that touch, such as a pan and a steak.

review.q: A cook boils pasta in a pot too small for it, and the pieces stick together. Why?
choices: The pasta was too fresh
Too little water dropped back to a simmer and stopped circulating, so pieces glued together
The water was too hot
The salt made it sticky
review.why: Boiling is convection. Enough water at a rolling boil keeps the pasta moving and the temperature steady.

review.q: Which food is a poor match for the broiler?
choices: A three-pound beef chuck roast
A thin flank steak
Sliced zucchini
A salmon fillet
review.why: Broiling is fast, intense heat from one side. A large tough roast needs slow moist heat such as braising.

review.q: Which of these is a combination cooking method?
choices: Roasting
Steaming
Grilling
Braising
review.why: Braising browns with dry heat and finishes with moist heat under a lid.

review.q: Roasted vegetables came out pale and watery. What is the single most likely cause?
choices: The oven was too hot
Too much salt
The pan was crowded so the food steamed
The vegetables were cut too large
review.why: Crowding traps steam and holds the surface at 212 °F, where nothing browns.

review.q: Why do most recipes say to reduce the oven by about 25 °F when using a convection fan?
choices: Moving air transfers heat faster, so the same setting would overcook
The fan makes the oven colder
Convection ovens read 25 °F high
The fan dries the food out unless the oven is cooler
review.why: Circulating air strips away the cool layer around food and cooks faster, so a lower setting gives the same result.

review.q: A cook sears a pork chop and leaves the browned bits in the pan. What are they called and what are they for?
choices: Char, and they should be thrown away
Fond, and they are the base of a pan sauce
Gelatin, and they thicken soup
Caramel, and they go in dessert
review.why: Fond is the flavorful browned residue from searing. Deglazing with liquid lifts it into a sauce.

review.q: A grease fire starts in a sauté pan. What should the cook do?
choices: Pour water on it
Carry the pan to the sink
Fan it with a towel
Slide a lid over the pan and turn off the burner
review.why: Smother a grease fire with a lid or baking soda and cut the heat. Water spreads burning grease, and moving the pan spreads the fire.
